tagline: Schools and railroad history behind a string of Louisiana place names
intro: Grand Coteau retains Victorian buildings from its nineteenth-century growth, while the railroad divides Scott. Louisiana Highway 93 passes through the center of Scott and meets Highway 723 in Ossun, three miles north.

Grand Coteau’s earlier community, Buzzard Prairie, served travelers between Washington and St. Martinville in the early nineteenth century. By 1880, Scott had a completed train depot and had become a village. Its 1907 incorporation brought the name of Southern Pacific division superintendent J. B. Scott.

The names along the journey supply their own landmarks: Grand Coteau means great hill; Cankton honors physician Dr. Cank; Ossun takes its name from a place in France near Lourdes. At Scott, U.S. 90 runs through the heart of town as Cameron Street.

moments.title: Grand Coteau
moments.text: Schools gave Grand Coteau an earlier name, St. Charles Town. In 1821, two nuns of the Religious of the Sacred Heart established a convent and school after Mrs. Charles Smith donated land, a building and their travel expenses. Jesuits founded St. Charles College in 1837. The original college building was destroyed by fires in 1900 and 1907; the present building dates to 1909. The campus continues to train Jesuits and also serves as a retreat center and home for elderly Jesuits. The Academy of the Sacred Heart remains a girls’ school, alongside the boys’ Berchmans Academy established in 2006.

moments.title: Cankton
moments.text: Cankton bears the nickname of a physician, Dr. Lois Aristide Guidry, known as Dr. Cank. After earning his medical degree at Tulane, he practiced in the community then known as Coulee Croche. His first office was on Guidry Street. As his practice grew, he built a larger office on Main Street beside the home he shared with his wife, Cecile. Guidry died in 1951; the village incorporated under his nickname in 1960. The incorporated community then consisted of an elementary school, a Catholic church, a grocery store and several homes. His Main Street office survives.

moments.title: Scott
moments.text: The railroad still cuts Scott in two, a visible connection to the village’s beginnings. The depot was complete by 1880, and incorporation followed in 1907. The name honored J. B. Scott, a Southern Pacific division superintendent. The line is now Union Pacific, formerly Southern Pacific. Another official title arrived on April 12, 2012, when the Louisiana State Legislature designated Scott the Boudin Capital of the World. That title refers to Cajun sausage. Broussard, in the same parish, became the former Boudin Capital of the World, while Jennings claimed the Boudin Capital of the Universe.
